source: Chi, Feltovich, Glaser (1981) Categorization and representation of physics problems by experts and novices
finding: Founding result as reported by Mason and Singh (2011). Eight novices sorted by surface terms. Experts sorted by physics principle.
numbers: 8 calculus-physics novices vs 8 PhD-student experts. Novices used springs 75%, inclined plane 50%, kinetic energy 50%, pulleys 38%. Experts used springs 25%, none of the other three. Original paper was paywalled (HTTP 403); numbers taken from secondary source b02.
limits: Tiny sample. Exact written instructions and most problems are lost. Experts were graduate students, not professors.
agent_relevance: The sorting contrast is the root of the S0 gate idea: classify a problem by its principle before attacking it. But the base evidence is 16 people.

source: Mason and Singh (2011) Assessing expertise in introductory physics using categorization task, Phys Rev ST PER 7, 020110
finding: Large classroom near-replication of Chi et al. Found a wide spread of expertise, with big overlap between introductory students and graduate students. Faculty beat graduate students.
numbers: 3 classes of over 100 students each, 25 mechanics problems. 21 graduate students, 7 faculty. None of Chi's 8 novices chose expert categories; here 18% chose Newton's second law, 31% energy, 28% circular motion, 44% linear kinematics (on the 7 Chi problems). Mean share of problems in good categories: calculus-based 34.4%, algebra-based 18.7%.
quote: Our findings, which contrast with those of Chi et al.
limits: Classroom setting with concurrent course, not volunteers. Instructions differed. Only 7 of Chi's problems were still available. Categories were rated good/moderate/poor by the authors with faculty validation.
agent_relevance: Expertise is a distribution, not two types. A gate that assumes one clean novice or expert style per problem or per solver is too crude.

source: Mason and Singh (2011) same paper: surface-category prevalence
finding: Surface categories ('ramp', 'pulley') were much rarer in 2011 students than in the 1981 novices. Authors offer curriculum change after Chi as one possible reason.
numbers: Inclined plane was chosen significantly less often than in Chi (Chi novices 50%). Chi problems were harder for students: placed in good categories less often than the other problems.
limits: Cause not tested. Could also be instruction wording or in-class sampling.
agent_relevance: Surface-sorting is not a fixed trait of novices. It moves with training and with the task wording, so the effect of an instruction in our gate prompt may be large.

source: Wolf, Dougherty, Kortemeyer (2012) Empirical approach to interpreting card-sorting data, Phys Rev ST PER 8, 010124
finding: Replication at Michigan State using Chi's protocol. Simple descriptive statistics (number of categories, etc.) did not separate experts and novices. Most variation came from a 'stacker' versus 'spreader' sorting style, not from expertise.
numbers: 18 physics professors and 23 novices, 50 cards. Principal components: first component tracks stacker/spreader, not expertise. Expertise appears only on the second component (about 87% of variability sits in the first two).
quote: More often than not, attempts to repeat it fail
limits: One university. Authors note informal reports that most attempts to repeat Chi fail and are unpublished.
agent_relevance: Do not read sorting behaviour as an expertise signal without controlling style. For our agent: a sorting step needs a forced granularity or it measures habit.

source: Wolf, Dougherty, Kortemeyer (2012) Rigging the deck: selecting good problems for expert-novice card-sorting experiments, Phys Rev ST PER 8, 020116
finding: Whether a card-sort separates experts from novices depends strongly on which problems are in the set. Some 5- and 10-problem subsets separated them almost totally; others not at all.
numbers: 40,000 five-problem and 275,000 ten-problem subsets of a 50-problem set were tested. Full set: Cramer p about 0.048, Hotelling p<1e-5. Singh's 25-problem subset: Cramer p about 0.041. Problem features explained only 42.7% of discrimination variance; chapter spread (a proxy for deep structure) mattered most.
limits: Same 41 sorters as the previous line. Subset search is post hoc, so optimized sets are tuned to this sample.
agent_relevance: The gate's value depends on the problem mix, not just the model. Test on problem sets where principle and surface are crossed (orthogonal).

source: Veldhuis (1986/1990) Differences in the categorization of physics problems by novices and experts
finding: Early replication with crossed design. Sets 1 and 2 (Chi-like end-of-chapter problems) were inconclusive. Sets 3 and 4, built so each problem had one principle and one surface feature, agreed with Chi.
numbers: 94 novices, 5 intermediate, 20 physics professors; four problem sets. Detail taken from Wolf et al. 2012 (opened); the ERIC page gave an abstract only.
limits: Secondary report. Later work (Mason and Singh) says advanced novices show both deep and surface structure.
agent_relevance: Crossed principle-by-surface sets are the design that works. Use them to test our gate.

source: Schoenfeld and Herrmann (1982) Problem perception and knowledge structure in expert and novice mathematical problem solvers (ERIC ED200609)
finding: Replicated the Chi result in college mathematics. Experts sorted by mathematical principle, novices by surface form.
numbers: Experiment 1: 9 mathematics professors and 19 undergraduates sorted 32 problems. Strong-agreement pairs (agreed by two thirds): experts 10, novices 4, t(26)=10.45, p<.01. Clusters homogeneous in deep structure: experts 8 of 11 (73%), novices 5 of 10 (50%).
quote: reproduces mathematics problems the findings obtained previously with physics problems
limits: Small samples. A priori surface/deep labels by the authors. Hierarchical clustering on a similarity matrix.
agent_relevance: First replication outside physics, in the domain closest to our schema. Gives a prior that a principle-first sort exists for math too.

source: Schoenfeld and Herrmann (1982) Experiment 2: training changes perception
finding: A term-long problem-solving course moved novices toward expert-like sorting. A matched programming course did not.
numbers: 11 trained students vs 8 controls. Between-group sorting correlation fell from r=.650 (pre) to r=.492 (post, p<.01). Homogeneous deep-structure clusters: trained group 6 of 8 (75%) vs novices before 50%, experts 73%. Problem-solving gain F(1,17)=67.2 to 92.4 depending on scoring.
limits: Not randomised: students chose courses. 19 students. Post-instruction sorting still not truly expert-like, per authors.
agent_relevance: Sorting by structure is trainable, and it moves with problem-solving skill. A memory of solved problems keyed by principle may be the lever.

source: Hardiman, Dufresne, Mestre (1988/1989) The relation between problem categorization and problem solving among novices and experts, Mem Cogn 17, 627 (ERIC ED294753)
finding: Experiment 1, similarity-judgment task with surface and deep structure crossed. Experts chose the deep match more often than novices, but surface similarity also hurt experts.
numbers: 45 novices (B or better in mechanics), 8-10 experts. Deep-structure choice: experts 78%, novices 59%, F(1,53)=28.78, p<.0001. Novices correct with surface-only lure (S-D) 40% vs 77% when surface was neutral; S-D 95% CI 20-32% (not 0). Correlation of categorization score with problem-solving score r=.30, p=.042.
quote: surface features do interfere with their performance
limits: Reports 8 experts in methods and 10 in results. Small expert group. Physics mechanics only.
agent_relevance: Even experts are pulled by surface lures. A gate that trusts a first-glance sort will inherit that error. Crossed-lure test items are the right probe.

source: Hardiman, Dufresne, Mestre (1989) Experiment 2: novice subgroups by reasoning
finding: Novices who attempt principle-based reasoning solve more problems, even when the principle they name is often wrong.
numbers: 44 novices, 7 experts. Deep-match accuracy: experts 95%, novices 62% (surface group 56%, mixed 63%, principle group 69%). Groups n=17, 16, 11. Principle use: 70%, 23%, 6% of items. Principles named wrongly 38% of the time by principle group. Problem-solving score: surface 14%, mixed 32%, principle 57% correct.
limits: Correlational. Groups defined by reasoning style, not assigned. Small cells.
agent_relevance: Strong hint for S0: the act of naming a principle matters more than naming it right. Make the model state a candidate principle, then verify by checks (G2, G3), not by trusting it.

source: Hardiman (1988) Recognizing similarities between fraction word problems (ERIC ED299146)
finding: Four studies of fraction word problems. Novices lean on surface similarity but can pick structure-matches once some structure is held constant. Author proposes a third level between surface and deep.
numbers: Better solvers (0-1 errors) 84% correct on similarity items vs 66% for weaker solvers (2-5 errors), t(38)=3.37.
limits: Skimmed in part; four studies with different samples. Abstract and key tables read.
agent_relevance: Surface/deep is a two-level simplification. For math word problems an intermediate 'problem type' layer (operation structure) may be the usable signal.

source: Mestre, Dufresne, Gerace, Hardiman (1988) Promoting expert-like behavior among beginning physics students (ERIC ED294751)
finding: Five hours in a tool that forced a principle-first hierarchy raised deep-structure categorization, but did not raise problem solving beyond controls.
numbers: 42 students, 3 groups. Deep-structure choices: tool group 56% to 66%, equation-sort group 61% to 61%, textbook group 62% to 58%. Tool group S-D items 17% to 34%. Problem-solving test pre/post: tool 29.4 to 41.3, equation tool 36.4 to 44.9, textbook 31.6 to 44.4 (all similar gains).
limits: One short intervention, no feedback to students. Problem-solving gain similar in all groups, so no transfer shown. Mostly descriptive.
agent_relevance: Evidence against assuming that a better sort gives better solving. A principle-first gate must be tested for solve-rate, not for sort quality.

source: Rottman, Gentner, Goldwater (2012) Causal systems categories: differences in novice and expert categorization of causal phenomena, Cogn Sci
finding: Outside physics: novices sorted real-world phenomena by content domain, experts by causal structure (feedback vs chain).
numbers: ERIC abstract only: novice groups sorted primarily by domain, expert group by causal category. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only, full text not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports a cross-domain structure gate (feedback, chain, constraint) not only physics principles.

source: Cole et al. (2023) A card-sorting tool to measure expert versus novice thinking in scientific research, CBE Life Sci Educ
finding: Faculty and postdocs used deep-feature sorts more than graduate and undergraduate students. Giving expert-style group names helped all groups but undergraduates did not reach expert levels.
numbers: ERIC abstract only: three groups; Advanced Placement Biology undergraduates were more expert-like than those without.
limits: Abstract only. Different domain (research design).
agent_relevance: Providing the category labels up front (a menu of principles) helps sorting; our gate could give the model a closed set of types instead of free naming.

source: Wolf, Dougherty, Kortemeyer (2012) literature summary of later replications (Singh; Lin and Singh)
finding: Competing explanation of null replications: card-sorting measures many things (style, problem choice, difficulty) besides expertise.
numbers: Summary: Singh found graduate students role-playing introductory students did better than real introductory students (TAs overestimate); Lin and Singh quantum study: 22 juniors and seniors vs 6 faculty, with no ideal grouping even among faculty.
limits: Secondary summary of Singh and Lin-Singh papers; those originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Experts disagree on a 'right' category for hard problems. Our gate needs a tie-break rule, not a single truth label.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC), ICML
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to a grade-school math problem cuts accuracy; fewer than 30% of base problems are solved consistently. This is the novice 'surface' pull, in a model.
numbers: 100 base problems, 4,000 sampled variants; code-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003. Macro accuracy under 30% for most prompts. Self-consistency (20 samples) adds over 11 points micro accuracy; answer present in the 20 samples 99.7% of the time; best macro accuracy still 45%.
limits: 2023 models, easy problems, one distractor sentence per item.
agent_relevance: Supports voting plus code-selection (G5), and an explicit instruction to ignore irrelevant facts. Gate should strip givens that no principle uses.

source: Shi et al. (2023) GSM-IC: mitigations
finding: Two prompt fixes helped: exemplars that contain distractors, and an instruction 'feel free to ignore irrelevant information'. Neither fully fixed it.
numbers: Instruction added to chain-of-thought, least-to-most and program prompts raised accuracy consistently; distractor exemplars did not hurt the original GSM8K score. Least-to-most had about double the macro accuracy of chain-of-thought on code-davinci-002 but was lower on text-davinci-003. Role-name overlap sent text-davinci-003 macro accuracy to 0 on problems with more than 2 steps.
limits: Effect depends on model family; ordering of methods flipped between models.
agent_relevance: Test the 'ignore irrelevant' line per model; do not assume it transfers.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2024/2025) GSM-Symbolic, ICLR 2025
finding: Changing numbers (not names) in GSM8K templates lowers accuracy and widens its spread. Adding one clause that looks relevant but is not (GSM-NoOp) cuts accuracy sharply for all models.
numbers: 25 models; 100 templates x 50 instances = 5,000 per benchmark. GSM8K score above the centre of the symbolic distribution for 21 of 25 models (possible contamination). GSM-NoOp drops: Phi-3-mini 65.7 points, GPT-4o-mini 40.0, GPT-4o 32.0, o1-mini 29.1, o1-preview 17.5.
limits: Interpretation as 'no real reasoning' is contested; stronger models lose less. Authors' own controls suggest names matter little.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of the novice surface-cue effect. Newer reasoning models are more robust but not immune, so a relevance filter is still worth testing.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2024/2025) GSM-Symbolic: few-shot repair test
finding: Showing 8 solved variants of the same question, or 8 other NoOp questions, did not repair the NoOp drop.
numbers: NoOp-Symb: 8 shots of the same question from GSM-Symbolic; accuracy stayed within one standard deviation of the unrepaired NoOp score. NoOp-NoOp shots: Llama-3-8B unchanged, Phi-3 slightly lower.
limits: Only a few models tested in this control.
agent_relevance: Examples alone do not install 'principle-first' reading. The structure step must be explicit, not implied by exemplars.

source: Li et al. (2024) GSM-Plus: robustness benchmark for LLMs as math problem solvers
finding: Eight perturbation types on GSM8K seed questions, including distractor insertion and critical-thinking variants. Models lose accuracy on perturbed versions of problems they had solved.
numbers: 25 LLMs, 4 prompting methods. GPT-4: GSM8K 93.25, GSM-Plus 85.58, performance drop rate 8.23%. GPT-3.5-turbo: 73.62 to 61.19 (drop rate 16.88%). Human reference: 96.77 to 98.75.
limits: Perturbed questions were written by GPT-4 and human-checked; some were wrong.
agent_relevance: A cheap regression test for our gate: same problem, perturbed surface, same answer.

source: Huang et al. (2025) MATH-Perturb: benchmarking LLMs' math reasoning against hard perturbations
finding: Hard perturbations (problems that look the same but need a different method) lower accuracy; simple perturbations do not. Models sometimes force the old solution pattern onto the new problem.
numbers: 279 level-5 MATH problems, each with a simple and a hard variant. o1-mini fell 16.49 points and Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking fell 12.9 points on hard variants (Gemini: 92.47 original, 78.14 hard). Final-answer copying (mode collapse) explains under 10% of errors for most models.
limits: Small set; some models may have seen the originals. In-context original solution can mislead on hard variants.
agent_relevance: Mirror image of the novice error: the model sorts by surface and reuses a recalled schema when structure has changed. A schema match should be checked against the stated givens before reuse.

source: Huang et al. (2025) MATH-Perturb: in-context original solution
finding: Showing the solution to the original problem helped on simple variants but could mislead on hard variants.
numbers: Authors count problems turned wrong versus right by the example (misleading vs ICL effect); manual repeat trials: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 50% pass on one problem with 30% of its errors due to memorized pattern; o1-mini 75% pass, all errors the same memorization.
limits: Anecdotal case counts in the figure examples.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of a similar solved problem (our memory) is a double-edged tool. Retrieved schemas need a fit test.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR
finding: Prompting the model to recall relevant problems and a short tutorial before solving beats zero-shot and few-shot chain-of-thought on math and code. Generating the tutorial first aligns recalled examples to method, not wording.
numbers: Manual check of 100 cases (50 correct, 50 wrong): of correct, 35/50 had relevant and correct recalled exemplars, 9 relevant but wrong, 6 irrelevant. Of wrong, 28/50 had good exemplars but the model failed, 12 of those from a generalization gap. Best at K=3 to 5 exemplars. Codeforces: self-generated knowledge added gains over exemplars alone.
limits: Self-generated exemplars can be wrong; small models do better with retrieved exemplars. Table values not copied here (layout unreadable).
agent_relevance: Model-made principle recall is plausible but unverified (G2). Use it only with a check.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction, ICLR
finding: Asking for the governing principle first, then reasoning from it, helps physics and chemistry. Most remaining errors are in reasoning, not in finding the principle.
numbers: PaLM-2L on MMLU physics 66.4% to 73.2%, chemistry 70.9% to 81.8% (5-run means). Step-back fixes 20.5% of baseline errors but adds 11.9% new ones. Over 90% of remaining errors are at the reasoning step; principle errors are rare.
limits: Same model family (PaLM-2L, GPT-4, Llama2-70B); gains smaller for GPT-4. 11.9% new errors is a real cost.
agent_relevance: A direct LLM version of the expert principle-first move: cheap, positive, but costs about 12 points of new errors. Gate only when a signal says so (G1).

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts, NeurIPS
finding: A library of distilled problem-class templates, retrieved per problem, beat prior prompting methods at lower cost.
numbers: 10 reasoning tasks. Gains over previous best: Game of 24 +11%, Geometric Shapes +20%, Checkmate-in-One +51%; cost about 12% of multi-query methods.
limits: Authors' own benchmark choice; gains largest on puzzle-like tasks with fixed solution classes.
agent_relevance: Template memory keyed by problem class is the closest published form of an expert schema store.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive capabilities of LLMs: an exploration in mathematical problem solving
finding: GPT-4 labelled math problems with skills, clustered them, and examples chosen by skill label beat random, topic-based and complexity-based selection.
numbers: On MATH: +11.6% over chain-of-thought, +3.5% over Complex CoT and over topic-based examples. Program-aided prompts +7.52% over PAL on 500 MATH items. Skill-based beat random in 11 of 18 skills on GSM8K. Labels from GPT-4 also helped Mixtral.
limits: Preprint, under review at the time. One strong labeller. Gains smaller against topic-based baseline.
agent_relevance: Skill labels beat coarse topics: evidence that fine-grained 'deep' typing is worth more than surface topic. Needs a G3-style held-out test.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogies in unfamiliar alphabets: humans stayed high, GPT models fell sharply. Suggests reliance on similarity to training data.
numbers: 136 human participants (1,876 samples); mean counterfactual accuracy: humans 75.3%, GPT-3 48.8%, GPT-3.5 35.0%, GPT-4 45.2%. Human accuracy stayed flat as permuted letters grew.
limits: Older GPT models; letter-string domain; later reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Structure transfer is weak when surface changes. Probe the gate with surface-shifted twins.

source: Sourati et al. (2023/2024) ARN: analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: LLMs pick near-surface matches over structural (system) matches. On far analogies GPT-4 scored below chance, with near distractors worse.
numbers: Humans: 96% overall; 94.1% far analogies; 97.9% near. Models: 39.6% on far analogies (chance 50%), 33.9% when a far analogy faces a near distractor, 75.0% on near analogies. GPT-4 mean 68.1%. Solved examples and chain-of-thought helped far analogies but cost near ones.
limits: Narratives and proverbs, not math. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Direct model-side replication of the surface-over-system pull. Few-shot trade-off: examples help far cases and hurt near ones.

source: Mason and Singh (2011): boundary on who counts as expert
finding: Who counts as an expert changes the finding. PhD students were Chi's experts; faculty sorted significantly better than graduate students, and calculus-based students overlapped with graduate students.
numbers: 21 graduate students and 7 faculty vs introductory groups; authors say faculty beat graduate students; also note Chi's 'elegance' criterion for expert categories was disputed by several faculty.
limits: Faculty n=7. Panel ratings by authors.
agent_relevance: Our reference standard for a good sort should come from checked solutions, not from a label of 'expert'.

source: Mason and Singh (2011): rival explanation from Keith
finding: Reported by Mason and Singh: novices who explicitly used a general problem-solving strategy sorted more expert-like. Keith's own paper was not opened.
numbers: Keith's strategy was taught over an algebra-based physics course, with few students. No number given in the source.
limits: Secondary report. Small sample.
agent_relevance: Supports a taught procedure (explicit principle step) over innate novice style.
